claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance in multiprincipal-element alloys is governed by competition between rapid Mn transport and slower Cr and/or Al transport.
In the Cantor alloy, Mn diffuses outward faster than Cr.
Al diffuses more slowly than Mn under the proposed oxidation conditions.
Differential outward cation diffusion produces a layered scale with an outer Mn-rich oxide and an inner Cr-rich oxide in CoCrFeNiMn-type alloys.
The Mn-rich outer oxide is porous and non-protective.
Rapid Mn oxidation depletes Mn near the interface, promotes pore formation, and accelerates oxide growth.
A continuous, dense, adherent Cr2O3 and/or Al2O3 inner layer acts as the principal barrier to oxygen and cation transport.
Oxide-scale composition, compactness, adhesion, and growth kinetics largely determine alloy durability during oxidation.
Cr and Al additions can promote thermodynamically stable protective Cr2O3 and Al2O3 scales, respectively.
The proposed initial material can be a homogeneous equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy or a FeNiCuAl-based alloy in an as-cast or thermally homogenized state.
Reducing Mn concentration while holding Cr and Al constant will suppress Mn transport during oxidation.
Additional alloying elements can be selected to act as barriers to Mn diffusion.
Layered oxide formation occurs in CoCrFeNiMn at 900-1100 degrees Celsius in 20% O2/80% N2.
Oxidation for hours to 120 hours at 900-1100 degrees Celsius promotes scale formation under equilibrium conditions.
Suppressing Mn diffusion will produce a thinner, more uniform, more adherent scale with less Mn oxide and more prominent Cr2O3 and/or Al2O3.
Suppressing Mn diffusion will improve oxidation resistance relative to the unmodified baseline.
The baseline alloy has a relatively thick, porous Mn-rich outer scale and a less effective protective inner layer because Mn diffusion is uncontrolled.
The proposed mechanism should apply to comparable multication alloys between approximately 900 and 1100 degrees Celsius in oxidizing environments.
At lower temperatures or substantially different oxygen partial pressures, diffusion kinetics and oxide-formation mechanisms may differ markedly.

Failure of the Mn-suppressed alloy to show a statistically significant reduction in scale thickness, improved compactness or adhesion, or a more prominent Cr/Al-rich inner layer would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field permits a generic FeNiCuAl-based alloy, which need not contain Mn, while the intervention and baseline require suppressible Mn transport and a Mn-rich outer scale. The comparison is therefore not internally applicable to every stated initial alloy.
